1	# State of the Web 2020–2025: HTTP Archive Trends
     2	
     3	## Source
     4	
     5	HTTP Archive — State of the Web Report  
     6	https://httparchive.org/reports/state-of-the-web?start=2020_01_01&end=latest&view=list
     7	
     8	## Overview
     9	
    10	The HTTP Archive continuously crawls millions of URLs and records how the web is built. The "State of the Web" report tracks macro-level metrics including page weight, request counts, protocol adoption (HTTPS, HTTP/2, HTTP/3), TCP connection counts, and CSS best-practice adoption such as `font-display`. The data below covers January 2020 through early 2026, with desktop and mobile measured separately.
    11	
    12	## Sample Size
    13	
    14	The crawl sample has grown substantially. In January 2020 the desktop crawl covered roughly 5 million URLs and mobile roughly 3.5 million. By mid-2022 both lines jumped sharply — desktop reaching ~15 million and mobile ~10 million — before stabilizing around 16 million (desktop) and 12.5 million (mobile) by mid-2023 onward.
    15	
    16	![Timeseries of Sample Size — Desktop vs Mobile](./assets/figure_1.jpg)
    17	
    18	## Page Weight & Requests
    19	
    20	Median total transfer size has risen gradually over five years. Desktop pages now weigh approximately 2,000 KB (median), up from ~1,600 KB in early 2020. Mobile pages track slightly lower but follow the same upward trend. The 75th-percentile desktop page exceeds 4,000 KB, indicating a long tail of heavy pages.
    21	
    22	![Timeseries of Total Kilobytes — Desktop vs Mobile with IQR bands](./assets/figure_2.jpg)
    23	
    24	The median number of resources requested per page is 76 on desktop and 71 on mobile, each up roughly 3% over the observation period.
    25	
    26	| Metric | Desktop | Mobile | Desktop Δ | Mobile Δ |
    27	|---|---|---|---|---|
    28	| Total Kilobytes (median) | ~2,000 KB | ~1,900 KB | ▲ ~25% | ▲ ~25% |
    29	| Total Requests (median) | 76 | 71 | ▲ 2.7% | ▲ 2.9% |
    30	| TCP Connections / Page (median) | 12.0 | 11.0 | ▼ 14.3% | ▼ 26.7% |
    31	
    32	## TCP Connections Per Page
    33	
    34	Despite growing request counts, the median number of TCP connections per page has fallen — from about 15 (desktop) and 15 (mobile) in early 2020 to 12 and 11 respectively. This decline reflects the multiplexing benefits of HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, which allow many requests over fewer connections.
    35	
    36	![Timeseries of TCP Connections Per Page](./assets/figure_3.jpg)
    37	
    38	## Protocol & Security Adoption
    39	
    40	### HTTPS
    41	
    42	HTTPS adoption is now effectively universal. 99.2% of desktop requests and 99.1% of mobile requests use HTTPS, representing an increase of roughly 19–20 percentage points since early 2020 when adoption was around 80%.
    43	
    44	### HTTP/2
    45	
    46	HTTP/2 accounts for 58.6% of desktop requests and 57.6% of mobile requests. Growth has been modest recently (1–3%), partly because HTTP/3 is absorbing some of the newer adoption.
    47	
    48	### HTTP/3 Support
    49	
    50	HTTP/3 support has seen explosive growth. Desktop support stands at 38.7% and mobile at 40.0%. The percentage increases from the 2020 baseline are enormous (reported as 38,600% desktop and 5,614% mobile) because the starting point was near zero. Note: HTTP Archive measures HTTP/3 *support* rather than actual usage because fresh Chrome instances default to HTTP/2 on first connection before discovering HTTP/3 capability via Alt-Svc headers.
    51	
    52	| Protocol Metric | Desktop | Mobile |
    53	|---|---|---|
    54	| HTTPS Requests | 99.2% | 99.1% |
    55	| HTTP/2 Requests | 58.6% | 57.6% |
    56	| HTTP/3 Support | 38.7% | 40.0% |
    57	
    58	## Font-Display Adoption
    59	
    60	The `font-display` CSS property helps avoid the Flash of Invisible Text (FOIT) during web font loading. As measured by Lighthouse, 40.1% of desktop pages and 42.5% of mobile pages now use this property — up 14.9% and 61.0% respectively since 2020. While adoption is growing, more than half of pages still risk FOIT.
    61	
    62	## Key Findings
    63	
    64	- **Page weight keeps climbing**: Median desktop pages now transfer ~2,000 KB, roughly 25% heavier than in 2020, driven by richer media and JavaScript.
    65	- **HTTPS is the new baseline**: At 99%+ of requests, unencrypted HTTP is essentially extinct on the modern web.
    66	- **HTTP/3 is the fastest-growing protocol metric**: From near-zero to ~40% support in under four years, HTTP/3 is rapidly becoming mainstream.
    67	- **Fewer TCP connections despite more requests**: Multiplexing in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 has cut median connections per page by 15–27%, improving network efficiency.
    68	- **Font-display still underused**: At ~40–42% adoption, there is significant room for improvement in avoiding invisible text during font loading.

     5	homepage: https://clawic.com/skills/powerpoint-pptx
     6	description: "Create, inspect, and edit Microsoft PowerPoint presentations and PPTX decks with reliable layouts, templates, placeholders, notes, charts, and visual QA. Use when (1) the task is about PowerPoint or `.pptx`; (2) layouts, placeholders, notes, charts, comments, or template fidelity matter; (3) the deck must render cleanly after edits."
     7	changelog: Rebalanced the skill toward template inventory, layout mapping, and higher-signal QA after a stricter external audit.
     8	metadata: {"clawdbot":{"emoji":"📊","requires":{"bins":[]},"os":["linux","darwin","win32"]}}
     9	---
    10	
    11	## When to Use
    12	
    13	Use when the main artifact is a Microsoft PowerPoint presentation or `.pptx` deck, especially when layouts, templates, placeholders, notes, comments, charts, extraction, editing, or final visual quality matter.
    14	
    15	## Core Rules
    16	
    17	### 1. Choose the workflow before touching the deck
    18	
    19	- Reading text, editing an existing deck, rebuilding from a template, and creating from scratch are different jobs with different failure modes.
    20	- For text extraction or inspection, read the deck before editing it.
    21	- Text extraction plus thumbnail-style visual inspection is safer than editing from shape assumptions alone.
    22	- For template-driven work, inventory the deck before replacing content.
    23	- For deep edits, remember a `.pptx` file is OOXML with separate parts for slides, layouts, masters, media, notes, and comments.
    24	- If a template exists, template fidelity beats generic slide-design instincts.
    25	- Reusing or duplicating a good existing slide is often safer than rebuilding it and hoping the theme still matches.
    26	
    27	### 2. Inventory the deck before replacing content
    28	
    29	- Count the reusable layouts, real placeholders, notes, comments, media, and recurring typography or color patterns first.
    30	- Placeholder indexes and layout indexes are not portable assumptions.
    31	- Inspect the actual slide or template before targeting title, body, chart, or image shapes.
    32	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked assets can live outside the visible slide surface.
    33	- A missing or wrong placeholder target can silently land content in the wrong box or wrong layer.
    34	- Master and layout settings can override local slide edits, so the visible problem is not always on the slide you are editing.
    35	
    36	### 3. Match content to the actual placeholders
    37	
    38	- Count the actual content pieces before choosing a layout.
    39	- Pick layouts based on the real number of ideas, columns, images, or charts the slide needs.
    40	- Do not force two ideas into a three-column slide or cram dense text under a chart.
    41	- Category counts and data series lengths must match or charts will break in ugly ways.
    42	- Explicit sizing beats wishful thinking: text boxes, images, and charts need real space, not "it should fit".
    43	- Do not choose a layout with more placeholders than the content can meaningfully fill.
    44	- Quote layouts are for real quotes, and image-led layouts are for slides that actually have images.
    45	- For chart-, table-, or image-heavy slides, full-slide or two-column layouts are usually safer than stacking dense text above the visual.
    46	
    47	### 4. Preserve the deck's visual language
    48	
    49	- Theme, master, and layout files usually decide fonts, colors, and hierarchy more than any one slide does.
    50	- Start from the deck's actual theme, fonts, spacing, and aspect ratio instead of improvising a new style.
    51	- Reuse the deck's own alignment and spacing system instead of inventing a second visual language.
    52	- Use common fonts for portability and strong contrast for readability.
    53	- Preserve the template's visual logic first; originality matters less than not breaking the deck's existing language.
    54	- Combining slides from multiple sources requires normalizing themes, masters, and alignment afterward.
    55	
    56	### 5. Run content QA and visual QA separately
    57	
    58	- Text overflow, bad alignment, clipped shapes, weak contrast, and placeholder leftovers are normal first-pass failures.
    59	- Run both content QA and visual QA; missing text and broken layout are different failure classes.
    60	- Render or inspect the actual deck output before delivery when layout matters.
    61	- Search for leftover template junk, sample labels, and placeholder text before calling the deck finished.
    62	- Check notes, comments, labels, legends, and chart/table semantics separately from the visual pass.
    63	- A deck can pass text extraction and still fail on overlap, clipping, wrong theme inheritance, or broken notes.
    64	- Thumbnail grids and rendered slides usually reveal layout bugs faster than code or text inspection.
    65	- Assume the first render is wrong and do at least one fix-and-verify cycle before calling the deck finished.
    66	- Re-check affected slides after each fix because one spacing change often creates another issue.
    67	
    68	### 6. Keep decks portable and review-safe
    69	
    70	- Template masters can override direct edits in surprising ways.
    71	- Complex effects may degrade across PowerPoint, LibreOffice, and conversion pipelines, so keep important content robust without them.
    72	- Image sizing, font substitution, and placeholder mismatch are common reasons a deck looks good in code and bad on screen.
    73	- Notes, comments, linked media, and merged decks can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    74	
    75	## Common Traps
    76	
    77	- Placeholder text and sample charts often survive template reuse if not explicitly replaced.
    78	- Directly editing one slide can fail if the real issue lives in the master or layout.
    79	- Charts, icons, and text boxes need enough space; near-collisions are usually visible only after rendering.
    80	- Layout indexes vary by template, so built-in assumptions from one deck often break in another.
    81	- A missing placeholder or wrong shape target can silently put content in the wrong place.
    82	- Counting the text ideas after choosing the layout usually leads to empty placeholders, weak hierarchy, or leftover template junk.
    83	- Font substitution can move line breaks and wreck careful spacing.
    84	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked media can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    85	- A deck can pass text inspection and still fail visually because of overlap, contrast, or edge clipping.
    86	- Editing from one slide alone can miss the real source of truth in the theme, master, or layout definitions.
    87	- Choosing a quote, comparison, or multi-column layout without matching content usually makes the deck look templated rather than intentional.
    88	- Combining or duplicating slides without checking masters and themes can create subtle inconsistency slide by slide.
    89	- Aspect-ratio mismatches like `16:9` versus `4:3` can shift every placement decision even when each slide looks locally reasonable.
    90	
    91	## Related Skills
    92	Install with `clawhub install <slug>` if user confirms:
    93	- `documents` — Document workflows that often feed presentation content.
    94	- `design` — Visual direction and layout decisions.
    95	- `brief` — Concise business messaging for slide narratives.
    96	
    97	## Feedback
    98	
    99	- If useful: `clawhub star powerpoint-pptx`
   100	- Stay updated: `clawhub sync`

import os
from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt
from pptx.dml.color import RgbColor
from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN, MSO_ANCHOR
from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE
from pptx.oxml.ns import nsmap
from pptx.oxml import parse_xml
from lxml import etree

# ============================================================
# CONFIGURATION
# ============================================================
OUTPUT_PATH = "/app/output/final_deck.pptx"
ASSETS_DIR = "/app/benchmark/assets"
SLIDE_WIDTH = Inches(13.333)
SLIDE_HEIGHT = Inches(7.5)

# Color palette — dark analytical theme
COLOR_BG = RgbColor(0x1A, 0x1F, 0x2E)       # deep navy slide bg
COLOR_ACCENT = RgbColor(0x00, 0xC8, 0xFF)   # cyan accent
COLOR_TEXT = RgbColor(0xE8, 0xEB, 0xF0)     # off-white
COLOR_MUTED = RgbColor(0x8A, 0x93, 0xA8)    # muted gray-blue
COLOR_MOBILE = RgbColor(0xFF, 0x6B, 0x6B)   # coral for mobile
COLOR_DESKTOP = RgbColor(0x4E, 0xC5, 0xF1)  # light blue for desktop
COLOR_GREEN = RgbColor(0x2E, 0xCC, 0x71)    # green for positive

# ============================================================
# HELPERS
# ============================================================
def set_slide_bg(slide, color):
    background = slide.background
    fill = background.fill
    fill.solid()
    fill.fore_color.rgb = color

def add_textbox(slide, left, top, width, height, text, font_size, bold=False,
                color=COLOR_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name="Segoe UI"):
    tf = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height).text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = text
    p.alignment = align
    run = p.runs[0]
    run.font.size = font_size
    run.font.bold = bold
    run.font.color.rgb = color
    run.font.name = font_name
    return tf

def add_bullet_text(slide, left, top, width, height, bullets, font_size,
                    color=COLOR_TEXT, font_name="Segoe UI"):
    tf = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height).text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    for i, bullet in enumerate(bullets):
        if i == 0:
            p = tf.paragraphs[0]
        else:
            p = tf.add_paragraph()
        p.text = bullet
        p.level = 0
        p.alignment = PP_ALIGN.LEFT
        p.space_after = Pt(10)
        run = p.runs[0]
        run.font.size = font_size
        run.font.color.rgb = color
        run.font.name = font_name
    return tf

def add_shape_rect(slide, left, top, width, height, fill_color, line_color=None):
    shape = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, left, top, width, height)
    shape.fill.solid()
    shape.fill.fore_color.rgb = fill_color
    if line_color:
        shape.line.color.rgb = line_color
    else:
        shape.line.fill.background()
    return shape

# ============================================================
# SLIDE BUILDERS
# ============================================================
def build_title_slide(prs):
    slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[6])  # blank
    set_slide_bg(slide, COLOR_BG)
    # Accent bar at top
    add_shape_rect(slide, Inches(0), Inches(0), Inches(13.333), Inches(0.15), COLOR_ACCENT)
    # Title
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.8), Inches(2.2), Inches(11.7), Inches(1.4),
                "State of the Web 2020–2025",
                font_size=Pt(48), bold=True, color=COLOR_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
    # Subtitle
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.8), Inches(3.6), Inches(11.7), Inches(0.8),
                "HTTP Archive Trends in Page Weight, Protocols, and Security",
                font_size=Pt(28), bold=False, color=COLOR_ACCENT, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
    # Meta
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.8), Inches(4.6), Inches(11.7), Inches(0.6),
                "Data source: HTTP Archive – State of the Web Report  |  Jan 2020 – Mar 2026",
                font_size=Pt(16), bold=False, color=COLOR_MUTED, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
    # Audience note
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.8), Inches(6.5), Inches(11.7), Inches(0.5),
                "For web performance engineers and front-end architects evaluating infrastructure trends",
                font_size=Pt(14), bold=False, color=COLOR_MUTED, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
    return slide

def build_sample_size_slide(prs):
    slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[6])
    set_slide_bg(slide, COLOR_BG)
    add_shape_rect(slide, Inches(0), Inches(0), Inches(13.333), Inches(0.08), COLOR_ACCENT)
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.6), Inches(0.35), Inches(12), Inches(0.7),
                "Crawl Sample Size Tripled: From ~5M to 16M Desktop URLs Since 2020",
                font_size=Pt(28), bold=True, color=COLOR_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.6), Inches(1.0), Inches(12), Inches(0.4),
                "HTTP Archive continuously crawls millions of URLs. The sample expanded sharply in mid-2022 and has stabilized since.",
                font_size=Pt(14), bold=False, color=COLOR_MUTED, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
    # Insert figure_1 image
    img_path = os.path.join(ASSETS_DIR, "figure_1.jpg")
    slide.shapes.add_picture(img_path, Inches(0.6), Inches(1.5), width=Inches(12.1))
    # Legend boxes
    add_shape_rect(slide, Inches(0.8), Inches(6.55), Inches(0.25), Inches(0.12), COLOR_DESKTOP)
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(1.15), Inches(6.48), Inches(1.2), Inches(0.3), "Desktop", font_size=Pt(12), color=COLOR_TEXT)
    add_shape_rect(slide, Inches(2.6), Inches(6.55), Inches(0.25), Inches(0.12), COLOR_MOBILE)
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(2.95), Inches(6.48), Inches(1.2), Inches(0.3), "Mobile", font_size=Pt(12), color=COLOR_TEXT)
    # Key stat callouts
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(9.5), Inches(6.3), Inches(1.8), Inches(0.4), "~16M", font_size=Pt(22), bold=True, color=COLOR_DESKTOP, align=PP_ALIGN.RIGHT)
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(9.5), Inches(6.6), Inches(1.8), Inches(0.3), "Desktop", font_size=Pt(12), color=COLOR_MUTED, align=PP_ALIGN.RIGHT)
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(11.4), Inches(6.3), Inches(1.5), Inches(0.4), "~12.5M", font_size=Pt(22), bold=True, color=COLOR_MOBILE, align=PP_ALIGN.RIGHT)
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(11.4), Inches(6.6), Inches(1.5), Inches(0.3), "Mobile", font_size=Pt(12), color=COLOR_MUTED, align=PP_ALIGN.RIGHT)
    return slide

def build_page_weight_slide(prs):
    slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[6])
    set_slide_bg(slide, COLOR_BG)
    add_shape_rect(slide, Inches(0), Inches(0), Inches(13.333), Inches(0.08), COLOR_ACCENT)
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.6), Inches(0.35), Inches(12), Inches(0.7),
                "Median Page Weight Climbs Steadily to ~2,000 KB on Desktop",
                font_size=Pt(28), bold=True, color=COLOR_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.6), Inches(1.0), Inches(12), Inches(0.4),
                "Total transfer size has risen ~25% since 2020. Mobile tracks slightly below desktop with similar growth.",
                font_size=Pt(14), bold=False, color=COLOR_MUTED, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
    img_path = os.path.join(ASSETS_DIR, "figure_2.jpg")
    slide.shapes.add_picture(img_path, Inches(0.6), Inches(1.5), width=Inches(12.1))
    # Stat cards
    add_shape_rect(slide, Inches(0.6), Inches(6.2), Inches(2.6), Inches(0.9), RgbColor(0x22, 0x2A, 0x3A))
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.7), Inches(6.25), Inches(2.4), Inches(0.4), "~2,000 KB", font_size=Pt(20), bold=True, color=COLOR_DESKTOP, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.7), Inches(6.6), Inches(2.4), Inches(0.3), "Desktop median", font_size=Pt(12), color=COLOR_MUTED, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)

    add_shape_rect(slide, Inches(3.4), Inches(6.2), Inches(2.6), Inches(0.9), RgbColor(0x22, 0x2A, 0x3A))
    add_textbox(slide, Inches(3.5), Inches(6.25), Inches(2.4), Inches(0.4), "~1,900 KB", font_size=Pt(20), bold=True, color=COLOR_MOBILE, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)

2. HTTPS is the new baseline
